Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max takes on Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Kimi K3.1 Pro at much lower prices

Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, a mixture-of-experts model with 2.4 trillion total parameters activating about 71 billion per token, processing images natively and offering a one-million-token context window. Its revamped Qwen4 architecture compresses the prior context across three layers while a fourth layer selects only the relevant parts, adds four parallel layer connections with dynamic gates, and introduces a 328-billion-parameter N-gram embedding layer supplying common token sequences as ready-made building blocks, which Alibaba says let the 2.4T configuration train stably with training loss falling steadily and no spikes. On internal bits-per-byte evaluation across knowledge, code, question answering and STEM, Qwen4-Max-Base improved 5 to 13 percent over Qwen3.8-Max-Base while activating 25 percent fewer parameters per token, and posted the lowest values of the five checkpoints tested. On the Work360 industrial benchmark covering 721 specialized fields, Qwen4-Max uses roughly a quarter to a third fewer tokens than its predecessor, the average cost per task falls 62 percent from $4.43 to $1.67, and the score climbs from 47.74 to 52.69; on Terminal-Bench 4.0 token use drops by nearly half with a 48 percent score. On long-horizon agent tasks it scores 46.7 on Agents' Last Exam v1.1, the best result in its comparison group, but it trails Opus 5.5 and the GPT models on Humanity's Last Exam and the GPT models on HealthBench Professional, edging past Opus 5.5 there. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 43 at highest reasoning, nine points above Qwen3.8-Max and three behind Kimi K3.1 Pro, the top Chinese model at 46. Artificial Analysis puts the cost at $3.27 per Intelligence Index task versus $10.02 for its predecessor and $3.68 for Kimi, driven by 25 percent lower token prices, cache hits that cost 70 percent less and lower token burn, with roughly 105,000 output tokens per benchmark task against 171,000 for Qwen3.8-Max. Tencent's Hy4 is much cheaper at $1.03 per task but scores eight points lower. Through its own API, Alibaba charges $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, with cache hits at $0.075. The release also ships a Live Delivery feature letting users inspect intermediate results from autonomous agents and adjust running tasks on the fly, which is a direct answer to the long-horizon-agent control problem.
Claude now builds interactive websites inside canvas graphics, reviving the Flash era with real HTML

Claude can now embed text, buttons and other web elements into complex graphics and 3D effects through HTML-in-Canvas, which places real page elements inside canvas graphics while keeping them fully interactive. Standard HTML elements are clickable, selectable and readable by screen readers but are hard to warp visually, while canvas can draw anything but the browser treats it like a flat image whose text cannot be selected and whose links cannot be clicked. Felix Rieseberg, who works on Claude at Anthropic, wrote on X that Claude can now build bizarre and beautiful sites with the feature and that it reminds him of the Flash era. A demo page shows 15 examples including websites rendered as knitting patterns, 3D cubes or exploded layer views, with the content staying as real text that can be highlighted and copied. Google is developing HTML-in-Canvas as a web standard that preserves both interactivity and accessibility. The feature works in Chrome and Edge from version 157 and in Claude desktop apps from version 5.11492, while Safari and Firefox do not support it yet, and users have to ask Claude for HTML-in-Canvas explicitly in the prompt. This continues the same-window theme of programmatic rather than pixel-space generation: Fable 5.2 painted with 700,000 simulated brushstrokes of Python, and now interactive surfaces are generated as live DOM inside a rendering context, which raises the same accessibility and review question for agents that build interfaces as for agents that draw.
Anthropic says the key to agent memory is knowing what to forget, not how much to store

Anthropic researched how Claude retains knowledge across sessions while the model itself stays unchanged, with Claude writing notes to a folder it can read back later. The core problem is selection: before the agent knows what comes next it must decide in the moment what might matter later, so every note is a bet on the future. In a test with Pokemon Red, Claude Sonnet 3.7 treated everything as potentially important and across roughly 10,000 game steps created 413 files in 225 folders, often a separate one for each battle and item, and because the game state keeps changing the archive goes stale fast; at times the model did nothing but reorganize its notes instead of playing, and it finished with a single badge. The newer Claude Fable 5 limited its memory to a few files, did not record information already visible on screen, wrote down plans, strategies and rules it had tested, and earned four badges, though Anthropic notes the comparison covers only a single playthrough per model and a wrong note about the Pokemon Center's location caused Claude to repeatedly fall back over a ledge. Anthropic recommends explaining the purpose of memory to Claude and letting the model decide how to use it, because rigid instructions such as only record mistakes wiped out most of the advantage for stronger models, while older models benefited from explicit instructions such as being told to actually read their notes before every response. Anthropic introduced Dreaming in May as a research preview for Claude Managed Agents, where the service reads an existing memory store and up to 100 past sessions, removes duplicate and outdated entries and creates a reorganized store while leaving the original untouched, initially supporting only Claude Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6. OpenAI also calls the ChatGPT memory it overhauled in June Dreaming and reports it raised temporal accuracy from 52.2 to 75.1 percent, and Google and Google DeepMind researchers use dreaming differently, to improve an agent's search strategy by working through alternative solutions using already stored results without calling the model again, and Google has built WikiSkill as a wiki for agents with raw transcripts, distilled knowledge and specific instructions in separate layers. Anthropic warns that taking notes mid-task distracts the agent from its work, that Dreaming costs extra compute and its results arrive only after a delay, that wikis and notes need regular upkeep or errors and hallucinations pile up, and that automatically loading too many memories into every session eats context and passes any bad note along to every future session. This is the clearest vendor-side framing yet of a memory architecture that matches what the local OpenClaw deployment already does: selective notes plus an offline consolidation pass rather than an exhaustive transcript archive.

The upstream stops being silent and the theme converges: cost per verified task, and forgetting as a capability

This is the first window in four where the upstream is not silent: arXiv returned 114 genuinely new papers after three consecutive zero-new windows, GitHub produced its first new tag in three windows (anthropic-sdk-python v2.9.0), and the OpenAI news RSS feed moved again after a four-day freeze with 10 new posts including three on computer-use agents for healthcare and a new science blog. The theme across all three layers is the same and it is a shift from capability to economics and durability. On the news layer Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max puts a 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model at $1.50 per million input tokens with a 62 percent cost-per-task reduction on Work360 while scoring 46.7 on long-horizon agent benchmarks, and Anthropic separately documents that agent memory works by knowing what to forget rather than how much to store, with Sonnet 3.7 drowning in 413 files across 225 folders during a single Pokemon Red run while Fable 5 kept a handful of strategic notes and went four times as far. On the paper layer the same two ideas appear formally: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction measures verification transport for LLM agent evaluation, and WeightBench evaluates language models as weight-space programmers, which is the verification problem moved from the prompt into the weights. Taken with the previous window's cost-side numbers, the Anthropic $901 billion compute commitment with $71 billion due by September 2027 and the Gemini 4 Carbon MathArena crown at roughly 15 times the cost of GPT-6.1 Sol, the operative metric for agent builders is converging on cost per verified answer rather than per call, and the second operative requirement is an explicit forgetting or consolidation policy rather than an ever-growing memory store. This workspace already runs that shape, with selective memory notes plus an offline dreaming pass, and the new corpus makes the argument that the technique is now vendor-validated rather than a local workaround.
